claims.text: Superconducting behavior in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level is determined by the cumulative d-electron contributions of the constituent elements in the disordered solid solution.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at% each.
The starting HEA is to be produced by arc melting followed by homogenization annealing.
The intervention increases the relative content of elements described as having high intrinsic density of states while preserving a single-phase solid solution.
Nb is an example of a constituent with high intrinsic density of states or robust d-electron density.
The local density of states at the Fermi level is influenced by interactions among the constituent elements and by chemical disorder.
Increasing the concentration of constituents with robust d-electron density raises the density of states at the Fermi level.
An elevated density of states at the Fermi level strengthens Cooper pairing.
Chemical disorder in the HEA enhances electron scattering.
The pairing enhancement caused by elevated density of states can prevail despite disorder-induced electron scattering.
Stronger Cooper pairing produced by elevated density of states increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Alloy variants enriched in high-density-of-states elements should have higher transition temperatures than the equiatomic baseline HEA.
The controlled baseline is an equiatomic HEA processed and tested under the same conditions as the compositionally modified variants.
The proposed density-of-states trend is restricted to single-phase, well-homogenized solid-solution HEAs without secondary-phase formation.
Formation of secondary phases or departure from a well-homogenized single-phase state may invalidate the predicted trend.

Failure of transition temperature to increase with high-density-of-states-element content, or failure of transition temperature to correlate with measured Fermi-level density of states, would falsify the hypothesis.
